article.title: What Inference Speedup Claims Disclose: MLPerf Rounds, Project Benchmarks and MLCommons' Planned Shift to Served-Endpoint Testing
article.summary: Independent coverage of MLPerf Inference v6.0 and v6.1 notes limits on comparing results, MLCommons says Endpoints will replace its datacenter benchmark, and project figures from vLLM and Valkey are self-reported.
article.body_markdown:
## Background

Two kinds of speedup figure circulate for LLM inference software. The first is published by the projects and vendors that build it. The vLLM project's [v0.32.0 release notes](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/releases/tag/v0.32.0), published October 18, 2026, attach throughput figures to many individual changes. Some name their conditions: a least-loaded API-worker change is credited with "43-85% more req/s on short requests (Qwen3-0.6B, 32 input / 1 output tokens) in the PR's benchmark", and an FP8 KV-cache default for GLM-5.x with "2.3-5.5% more throughput at a 7-11% TTFT cost in the PR's benchmark". Other lines give a figure without a setup, such as `fp8_ds_mla` on SM90 giving GLM-5.3-Flash "up to 31% more output throughput". The Machine Herald's [earlier briefing on the release](/article/2026-10/22-vllm-0320-drops-python-310-stops-allowing-every-cors-origin-by-default-and-removes-cascade-attention) recorded that no independent testing of those performance claims was found.

The Valkey project's [blog post](https://valkey.io/blog/kv-caching-on-valkey/), dated October 20, 2026, is a second example. It reports that two GPU nodes served about 25% more requests with a shared Valkey cache attached. It also describes the setup (100 concurrent conversations growing from 12K to 28K tokens of context, two nodes with 8 H100 GPUs each, Llama-3.1-70B on vLLM plus LMCache), says two settings were changed from their defaults, and states "The traffic is synthetic". The Herald's [earlier article](/article/2026-10/25-valkey-project-benchmarks-a-shared-valkey-kv-cache-for-llm-inference-reporting-25-more-requests-served-on-the-same-two-gpu-nodes) found no independent replication of that result.

The second kind is the consortium round. MLCommons published results for MLPerf Inference v6.0 on April 1, 2026, according to [The Decoder](https://the-decoder.com/nvidia-sets-new-mlperf-records-with-288-gpus-while-amd-and-intel-focus-on-different-battles/). The Herald [covered that round](/article/2026-04/21-mlperf-inference-v60-delivers-its-most-ambitious-benchmark-suite-yet-as-nvidia-triples-deepseek-r1-throughput-in-six-months) when it was published.

## Current situation

### What independent outlets say about comparing results

The Decoder's account of the v6.0 round says "the results are only partially comparable": Nvidia, AMD and Intel used different system configurations, models and scenarios, and "each company frames its numbers to put its own strengths front and center". It reports that AMD's submission for the Wan-2.2 text-to-video model was in the Open category rather than the Closed Division, "which formally limits direct comparability", and that AMD also cited post-deadline results and "notes these numbers weren't verified by MLCommons". It adds that Nvidia's reported 2.7x software improvement and AMD's reported 3.1x generational gain "measure fundamentally different things", one being software on the same hardware and the other a new chip architecture. Its overall reading is that MLPerf Inference "doesn't produce a straightforward leaderboard".

[Blocks & Files](https://www.blocksandfiles.com/ai-ml/2026/09/01/mlperf-storage-benchmark-updated-for-modern-ai/5293617) made a related point in a September 1, 2026 report on the MLPerf Storage v3.0 round, which added a KV-cache workload. It writes that "there is no one single result" and describes "suppliers being selective over their submitted workload results".

[StorageReview](https://www.storagereview.com/news/mlperf-inference-v6-1-5-7x-per-accelerator-gains-a-512-gpu-run-and-vera-rubins-first-peer-reviewed-numbers) covered MLPerf Inference v6.1 on September 16, 2026. It reports 30 submitting organizations and 486 datacenter and edge results, and that MLCommons says the best per-accelerator DeepSeek-R1 server result is 5.7x better than in v5.1 a year earlier. It labels the provenance of several figures. Nvidia's up to 2.5x token-throughput gain for Vera Rubin NVL72 over GB300 NVL72, obtained with TensorRT-LLM, and its up to 3.7x on a Qwen3 vision-language model, obtained with vLLM and NVIDIA Dynamo, are described as "NVIDIA's comparisons against its own prior generation". Intel's reported 2.4x Xeon 6980P gain on Llama 3.1-8B server throughput over v6.0 on identical silicon is called "a software-only gain". For AMD, the outlet summarizes that ROCm v7 software optimizations raised GPT-OSS-120B throughput on an eight-GPU MI355X node by 28% offline and 38% in the server scenario, and notes that a study commissioned from Signal65 reported lower operational cost per document and higher token output per dollar within fixed latency limits. It adds that AMD says comparable MI355X submissions from seven partners averaged within 4% of its reference system results, and that the DeepSeek-R1 run on Crusoe's 512-GPU MI355X cluster used SGLang with one eight-GPU replica per node.

### The shift to served-endpoint testing

StorageReview reports that 16 of the 30 v6.1 submitters used MLPerf's API-centric harness, "up from a single open-division submitter in v6.0", and that the harness "runs a true client/server setup over standard APIs against a hosted endpoint, which is how datacenter inference is deployed". It quotes David Kanter, head of MLPerf: "MLPerf Endpoints will replace Inference in our family of benchmarks for the datacenter". The outlet says Endpoints opens rolling submissions in October 2026 and replaces MLPerf Inference as the datacenter benchmark in 2027.

The MLCommons Endpoints policy repository gives the mechanics. The repository's [README](https://github.com/mlcommons/endpoints_policies) says v1.0 rolling submissions open on October 12, 2026. The [submission rules](https://github.com/mlcommons/endpoints_policies/blob/main/endpoints_submission_rules.md) describe a rolling model "suited to the faster cadence of Gen AI inference benchmarking" and say results are published bi-weekly, on the 1st and 3rd Wednesday of each month, and that a submitter may opt in to provisional publication, in which case results appear tagged "peer review pending" and the tag is removed at finalization. The accompanying [audit guidelines](https://github.com/mlcommons/endpoints_policies/blob/main/MLPerf_Endpoints_Audit_Guidelines.md), which describe checks that the audited system and software match those submitted, carry the warning "This is work in progress."

### A continuous benchmark outside the consortium

A third approach is the open-source [InferenceX](https://github.com/SemiAnalysisAI/InferenceX) project run by SemiAnalysis. Its README describes the project as continually benchmarking the most popular open-source inference frameworks, names SGLang, vLLM and TensorRT-LLM among the software stacks it tracks, and gives its rationale: "benchmarks conducted at a fixed point in time quickly go stale and do not represent the performance that can be achieved with the latest software packages." It says only results from its own repository are official. Its acknowledgements thank AMD for providing MI355X and CDNA3 GPUs and NVIDIA for access to a GB200 NVL72 rack and B200 GPUs, along with several cloud providers for compute.

## Implications

The sources identify several variables that decide whether two speedup figures can be compared. The Herald's reading of them is listed below; each item restates what a cited source reports.

- **Baseline.** A figure may compare a product with its own earlier software or generation, with a rival, or, as in the Valkey post's two test arms, with a run without the feature. StorageReview labels Nvidia's v6.1 gains as comparisons with its own prior generation, and The Decoder separates software gains on the same hardware from a new architecture.
- **Division and verification.** The Decoder points to the Open versus Closed distinction and to post-deadline numbers that MLCommons had not verified. The Endpoints rules add a "peer review pending" tag for results published before review finishes.
- **Selection of workloads.** The Decoder and Blocks & Files both report that submitters choose which tests to enter, so a leaderboard position applies only to the workloads actually submitted.
- **Software version.** Release cadence is part of the context. By the Herald's own calculation from the GitHub release timestamps, vLLM [v0.30.0](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/releases/tag/v0.30.0) (September 22), [v0.31.0](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/releases/tag/v0.31.0) (October 5) and v0.32.0 (October 18) were each 13 days apart. InferenceX says fixed-point benchmarks go stale, and the Endpoints rules describe a rolling model suited to a faster cadence.
- **Who ran the test.** vLLM's release notes and the Valkey post are project-authored. MLPerf entries are submitted by vendors and partners and then reviewed. InferenceX is run by a third party that discloses GPUs and compute provided by vendors and cloud providers.

For developers evaluating an inference engine, these sources imply that a speedup figure is most informative alongside its baseline, workload, engine version and review status. They also show where information is thin: the Herald found no independent replication of the vLLM per-change figures or the Valkey result, and in the MLPerf coverage reviewed, most speedup figures are attributed to the submitting companies.

## What the sources do not establish

None of the cited outlets reports an independent attempt to reproduce an MLPerf result outside the submitting organizations and their partners; the closest figures in the coverage are AMD's statements that partner submissions landed within 4% of its own. The MLPerf Endpoints v1.0 submission round opened on October 12, 2026, and the sources reviewed do not report v1.0 results. The audit guidelines are marked as work in progress, and the 2027 replacement date appears in StorageReview's report, while the Kanter quote it reproduces does not itself state a year. The comparison of InferenceX and MLPerf approaches in this article is a juxtaposition of their documentation; no source evaluates which gives more accurate figures.
